chapter: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
title: Playing with W. C. Handy on his only record
summary: He says he played with Handy in New York concerts and on the one St. Louis Blues record Handy made, which he calls the saddest record.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Didn't you have a picture taken with Eddie Heywood and W. C. Handy? Old man Handy, 'cause I know I had the picture of Handy.
I don't remember.
You played with Handy.
Yeah, we played here together. We played concerts here.
In New York?
Yeah.
But not in Atlanta?
No, no, no.
Did you know of W. C. Handy in Atlanta? Had you ever heard of him?
Yeah, I heard of him. I made the only record he ever made in his life.
No, but I mean while you were in Atlanta you heard of W. C. Handy?
I heard of him...
How did you hear of him?
Just like you talk about other people, you know.
I know, but I mean like, other musicians had told you about W. C. Handy?
Yes.
He was never through the towns when you were there?
No, I don't remember anything about it. The only thing I remember about him is the only record he ever made, I got it. He tried to play trumpet and I have it in my scrapbook.
What was the name of that?
'St. Louis Blues.'
That's the only record that W. C. made?
That's what he said and I got it written down right now in my book.
At that time...

Yes. That was made here in New York. He had the shakes; he couldn't play, you know. He was an old man, so he said he wanted to make a recording of his own before he passed, you know. So I have it written down...
And he said that that was the only recording?
That was the saddest record... (LAUGHTER)
